line: e4 Nf6 Qh5 c5 Qxc5 Nxe4 Qh5 Nc6
teaches: Against an early queen sortie, develop at the centre rather than hunting the queen. Every piece that comes out with a job keeps the queen short of safe squares by itself, and the side that spent its opening moves on one piece falls behind while you are simply playing chess.
explains: The knight comes to c6 covering d4 and adds a second developed piece while the enemy queen has moved three times and holds nothing. Chasing it directly would cost time of your own; this keeps every move useful, and the queen still has to find somewhere to stand.

line: e4 Nf6 Qh5 c5 Qxc5 Nxe4 Qh5 Nc6 Bc4 e6 Qf3 d5
teaches: The best central pawn move is the one that arrives hitting something. Building the centre and gaining a move are usually treated as separate goals, and when a single push does both, it is nearly always the move.
explains: The pawn steps to d5 and attacks the bishop on c4 while claiming the centre, so the bishop has to spend a move retreating and the centre gets built for free. That is the pattern to look for whenever an enemy piece has been posted on a diagonal a pawn can reach.
